title: Chapter 22: Handling Errors: try, except and Clear Messages
video_title: Python Chapter 22: Handling Errors, try, except and Clear Messages
summary: One damaged row crashed the Corner Cafe score board. Follow Asha as she catches errors with try and except, uses else and finally, asks again until an answer is valid, raises her own errors and tests them with pytest. Then watch her build a score loader with an AI assistant at all six stages, where her tests catch two confident AI mistakes.

scenes.title: Why this matters
scenes.direction: Define an exception, then real uses.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: An **exception** is an error while the program runs.
You have read exception reports since Chapter 9. Now you catch them.
Good programs expect bad data, say what happened, and carry on.

segments.say: An exception is an error that happens while a program runs, like a value error, or file not found.
You have read exception reports since Chapter 9. Now your program catches them, and decides what to do.
Customers type words instead of numbers. Files get deleted. Good programs expect this, and carry on when they can.

scenes.title: The idea: try, except, else, finally
scenes.direction: Teach the flow with the diagram and the table, then the analogy. Quiz on else. Breather.

visual.heading: Try first, catch if it fails
visual.label: The idea
body: `try` runs code that might fail. `except` catches the error it names.
visual.pre:
try:                     runs first
      score = int(answer)  if this fails ...
  except ValueError:       ... Python jumps here
      print("Please type a whole number.")
  else:                    only if nothing failed
      print("Saved.")
  finally:                 always, at the end
      print("Done.")

segments.say: A try block runs code that might fail. If an exception happens inside it, Python stops that block, and jumps to a matching except block.
The except line names the exception it catches. An exception of another type is not caught, and the program stops, as before.

visual.heading: Four parts, and when each one runs
visual.label: The idea
rows: Always first. It stops at the first exception.
Only when `try` finished with no exception.

segments.say: Try always runs first. It stops at the first exception.
Except value error runs only when a value error happened in try.
Else runs only when try finished with no exception at all.
And finally runs always, last, whatever happened.

visual.heading: Like a safety net
visual.label: Analogy
items: The act goes on as planned. The net catches only after a fall.
Unlike a real net, `except` catches only the error type it names.

segments.say: Think of the safety net under a trapeze. The act goes on as planned, and the net catches the artist only after a fall.
But a real net catches anyone. Except catches only the type of error it names.

visual.question: When does the `else` block run?
visual.explain: `else` runs only when the `try` block finished with no exception. `finally` is the part that always runs.

segments.say: Quick check. When does the else block run?

after.say: C. Only when try raised no exception. Finally is the one that always runs.

items: `try` runs code that might fail.
`except` catches the error it names.
`else` if nothing failed, `finally` always.

segments.say: Breather. Four parts, and you know when each one runs.
Next, Asha catches her first error.

scenes.title: Step 1: Catch a bad number
scenes.direction: Teach the jump before the ask. Ask which lines run for four. Reveal.

visual.heading: Step 1: Catch a bad number

segments.say: Step 1. In Chapter 4, int of the word two stopped the program with a value error. Line 2 holds three answers, and the loop tries each one.
Line 5 tries to turn the answer into a whole number. Line 6 prints it.
If line 5 fails, Python skips the rest of the try block, and jumps to the except block on line 7.

ask.question: For the answer `"four"`, which line prints: line 6, line 8, or both?

after.say: Only line 8. Line 5 failed, so line 6 never ran. And the loop went on with the next answer.
Int ignores the spaces around 3, as you saw in Chapter 4. And exclamation r, from Chapter 20, shows the quotation marks.

scenes.title: Step 2: else and finally
scenes.direction: Teach else and finally on a missing file. Ask what month.csv prints.

visual.heading: Step 2: else and finally

segments.say: Step 2. Line 7 reads a file. That can fail with file not found.
Lines 8 and 9 catch it, with a message.
Else, on line 10, runs only when the file was read. Finally, on line 12, runs every time.
Lines 16 and 17 call it twice: with week, and with month.

ask.question: What do the two lines for `month.csv` say?

after.say: No scores yet, then done. The except block ran, else was skipped, and finally ran anyway.
For week, else printed the file, and finally printed done.
Keep the try block small. Only the line that can fail belongs inside it.

scenes.title: Step 3: Ask again until it is valid
scenes.direction: Callback to Chapter 7. Try inside a while loop. Ask about the answer 7. Then a breather.

visual.heading: Step 3: Ask again until it is valid
visual.note: The user types: four, then 7, then 3.

segments.say: Step 3. In Chapter 7, a while true loop asked until the answer was valid. Now try sits inside the loop.
A word gives a value error, and line 7 asks for a whole number.
If the number is from 0 to 4, break ends the loop. Otherwise line 11 explains the range.

ask.question: The user types `7`. Which message does the program show?

after.say: Please type a number from 0 to 4. Seven is a whole number, so no exception. But the if on line 9 catches the wrong value.
Try catches an answer that is not a number. If catches a number outside the range. And each message says what to type next.

items: `except` catches the error it names.
`else` holds the code that needs success.
Try inside a loop, and ask again.

segments.say: Breather. A word no longer crashes Asha's program.
Next, Asha's own functions learn to refuse bad input.

scenes.title: Steps 4 and 5: Raise, and catch what you expect
scenes.direction: Teach raise and as error, then the bare except trap with a spot-it ask, then the specific version and a quiz.

visual.heading: Step 4: Raise your own error

segments.say: Step 4. A function can refuse bad input with raise. Line 4 creates a value error, with a message that names the price.
Line 11 catches it. As error keeps the exception in a variable called error.
Line 12 prints that message.

ask.question: Line 12 prints a message. What does it say?

after.say: Not saved: price cannot be negative: minus 1. The message from line 4 arrives at line 12.
A clear message names the problem and the value. Error, with nothing else, helps nobody.

visual.heading: Step 5: a bare except
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the output appears.

segments.say: Step 5. Line 7 is a bare except: no error type at all. It catches every exception, even the ones your own bugs cause.
Look closely at line 5.

after.say: It is refused too! Line 5 says anser, not answer. That name error was caught, and hidden.

visual.heading: The same code, catching ValueError only

segments.say: Now line 7 catches value error only. The spelling mistake is no longer hidden.
The report names line 5, and even suggests the right name. Catch the errors you expect from the data. Let your own bugs show.

visual.question: Which `except` line can hide a spelling mistake in your own code?
visual.explain: A bare `except:` catches every exception, including the `NameError` from a spelling mistake.

segments.say: Quick check. Which except line can hide a spelling mistake in your own code?

after.say: B. The bare except. It catches everything, including your bugs. It even catches Control C, the keys you press to stop a program.

scenes.title: Step 6: Test that an error is raised
scenes.direction: Callback to Chapter 19. pytest.raises on cafe_tools, then a version that forgets to raise. Ask, reveal, breather.

visual.heading: Asha's module, with the check

segments.say: Step 6. Asha keeps with tax in her cafe tools module, with the new check on lines 4 and 5.

visual.heading: Step 6: pytest.raises

segments.say: In Chapter 19, tests checked return values. Line 11 checks an error. The test passes only if line 12 raises a value error.
Both tests pass: two dots.

visual.heading: An older with_tax, with no check

segments.say: Here is an older with tax. Lines 5 and 6 have no check for a negative price.
The test on lines 9 to 11 is the same as before.

after.say: No. The function returned a value instead of refusing. Pytest reports: did not raise value error.

items: `raise` refuses bad input with a message.
Catch the error you expect, not every error.
`pytest.raises` checks that the error happens.

segments.say: Breather. You can catch, raise, and test errors.

scenes.title: Work with AI: a loader that handles every problem
scenes.direction: Safety first. Six stages on load_scores. Stage 3 plants the bare except around the loop; tests catch it; debug a short row; improve suggests except Exception.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: what could go wrong?
visual.label: Before you start
items: Ask the AI to list what could go wrong.
Make one test case for each problem, and run it.
A real score file is private: paste a made-up sample.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill: ask what could go wrong in your code.
Then make one test case for each problem, and run it.
And never paste private data. A real file of staff names is private, so paste a made-up sample.

visual.heading: Plan: what could go wrong?

messages.text: My function load_scores reads scores.csv and turns each score into an int. Do not write code yet. What could go wrong, and what should the program do each time?

1. The file is missing: FileNotFoundError. Give a message, return no scores.
2. A score is not a number: ValueError. Skip that row with a message.
3. The file has only the header: no error, return no scores.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha asks what could go wrong, and what the program should do each time. No code yet.
The AI lists three problems: a missing file, a score that is not a number, and a file with only the header.

visual.heading: Write it yourself, then check

messages.text: I wrote this myself. Do not rewrite it. Which lines handle problems 1 and 2?

Problem 1: lines 14 and 15 catch FileNotFoundError.
Problem 2: lines 12 and 13 catch ValueError for one row, so the loop goes on.

segments.say: Stage 2: write. Asha writes her own load scores first, and asks which lines handle each problem.
The AI names lines 12 to 15. That matches what she meant.

visual.heading: Generate: a loader from a request

messages.text: Write load_scores(path). It returns a list of (name, score). It must never crash, and it must skip a damaged row.
Here it is. It handles every problem, and it never crashes.

segments.say: Stage 3: generate. To compare, Asha asks the AI for the same function, from a short request.
The AI is sure: it handles every problem, and never crashes.

visual.heading: The AI's loader, on the damaged file

segments.say: Look where the try starts, on line 7, and where it ends. Lines 11 and 12 catch everything, and do nothing.
Line 17 loads the damaged file: Asha, Omar with three, and Lina.

ask.question: The AI says it handles every problem. Is it right?

after.say: No. Only Asha loads. The try block holds the whole loop, so Omar's row stopped it, and Lina was lost, with no message.
A better request names the exceptions to catch, and asks for a small try block.

visual.heading: Test: one case for each problem

messages.text: Give me test cases for load_scores. For each one, write the file contents and how many scores it should return.

1. Normal: Asha and Lina. Expect 2.
2. Damaged row: Asha, Omar with three, Lina. Expect 2.
3. Header only: expect 0.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks for test cases, each with the file and the number of scores it should return.
The AI lists three. They match the three problems from the plan.

visual.heading: The three cases, on the AI's loader

segments.say: She runs all three cases on the AI's loader. The damaged row case fails: it found 1 score, not 2.

visual.heading: Test: report the failure, ask for a fix

messages.text: The damaged row case fails: it found 1 score, not 2, with no message. Explain why, then fix it.

The try block holds the whole loop, so the damaged row stopped it. The bare except with pass hid the error.
Fix: a small try around one row, catching ValueError only, and a message for a missing file.

segments.say: Asha shows the AI the failing case, and asks for the cause, then a fix.
The AI explains: the whole loop was inside try, and the bare except hid the error. The fix puts a small try around one row, the same idea as Asha's own version.

visual.heading: The three cases, on the fixed loader

segments.say: She runs all three cases again, on the fixed loader. All three pass, and Omar's row gets a message.

visual.heading: Stage 5: a row with no score
visual.note: case_short.csv: Asha,4 then a row with only Ben, then Lina,4.

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. In a new test file, one row says only Ben, with no comma and no score. Her own version has the same gap.
Type error! The report points at line 11 of the loader: int of row score.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: A row in my file says only Ben. Now load_scores crashes on line 11 with: TypeError: int() argument must be a string, a bytes-like object or a real number, not 'NoneType'. Explain the cause first. Then show the smallest fix.

Ben's row has no score, so row["score"] is None, and int(None) raises TypeError.
Fix: catch both on line 12: except (ValueError, TypeError).

segments.say: Asha pastes the error, and asks for the cause first.
Ben's row has no score, so the value is None, and int of None raises a type error. The fix catches both errors as a tuple: the two names inside round brackets, like the tuples from Chapter 13.

visual.heading: All four cases, on the final loader

segments.say: She adds the short row as case 4, and runs every case again. All four pass.

visual.heading: Improve: one suggestion, then test it

messages.text: All four cases pass. Suggest one improvement, with one reason.
Use except Exception instead of except (ValueError, TypeError), so no future error can ever crash it.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one improvement.
The AI suggests: except Exception, so no future error can ever crash it.
Exception, with a capital E, is the parent of almost every error type. So except Exception catches nearly every error, your bugs included.

visual.heading: Except Exception, with a spelling mistake on purpose

segments.say: Asha tests the idea. She adds a spelling mistake on purpose: line 10 says scor, not score. Line 11 catches Exception.
Line 16 loads the normal file, with two good rows.

ask.question: Will Asha see her spelling mistake?

after.say: No. Every row is skipped with a wrong message, and the list is empty. The bug is hidden.

visual.heading: The same spelling mistake, with her specific except

segments.say: With her specific except, the key error stops the program, and points at line 10. She finds the spelling mistake at once. So she keeps the specific except.

visual.question: A score loader reads a file. Which `except` should catch a damaged score?
visual.explain: A damaged score raises `ValueError`. Catch that, and let other errors show your bugs.

segments.say: Quick check. A score loader reads a file. Which except should catch a damaged score?

after.say: D. Value error. That is the error a damaged score raises. Let every other error show.

items: Plan, write, generate, test, debug, improve.
A small `try` keeps one bad row from stopping the rest.
Test that a change does not hide your bugs.

segments.say: Breather. The AI made two confident mistakes, and Asha's tests caught both.
Next, four mistakes beginners make with try and except.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistakes 1 and 3 are spot-it asks. Mistakes 2 and 4 are explained.

visual.heading: Mistake 1: your turn to spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 1. You try. Line 4 turns the word four into a whole number. Line 5 catches an error.

ask.question: Will line 5 catch the error from line 4?

after.say: No. Int of four raises a value error, not a type error. So the program still stops.
after.heading: Mistake 1: catching the wrong type

after.say: The fix: catch the type the report names. Run the code once without try, to see it.

visual.heading: Mistake 2: a name that try never created

segments.say: Mistake 2. Line 4 failed, so score was never created. Line 7 still uses it: name error.
The fix: put the code that needs score in else.

visual.heading: Mistake 3: spot it
visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the error appears.

segments.say: Mistake 3. Remember the four parts. Look at what follows the try block.

after.say: An except or a finally block. Every try needs one, straight after it. Python cannot even read the file.
after.heading: Mistake 3: a try with no except

visual.heading: Mistake 4: raising text

segments.say: Mistake 4. Raise needs an exception, not text. Python stops with a type error.
The fix: put the message inside a value error.

items: Catch the type the report names.
Code that needs the result goes in `else`.
`raise` needs an exception, with a message.

segments.say: Last breather. Errors are now part of your plan, not a surprise.
Two questions to think about on your own come next.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: `try` and `except` catch an exception and show a clear message.
`else` runs when nothing failed. `finally` runs always.
Catch the exception you expect. A bare `except:` hides your bugs.
Keep each `try` block small.
`raise ValueError("message")` refuses bad input.

segments.say: Let's recap. Try and except catch an exception, and show a clear message.
Else runs when nothing failed. Finally runs always.
Catch the exception you expect. A bare except hides your bugs.
Keep each try block small.
Raise refuses bad input, with a message.
And pytest raises tests that the error happens.
